extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of a first serious year-long course in algebraic geometry (advanced undergraduates/graduate students and their teachers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and pedagogical/technical conventions for using or teaching Ravi Vakil's Foundations of Algebraic Geometry: recommended prerequisites, sequencing, emphasis, exercise policy, and choices about generality and hypothesis usage for a year-long foundations course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: This book has a lot of exercises. I have found that unless I have some problems I can think through, ideas don’t get fixed in my mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises are interspersed with the exposition (not left to the end); most have been field-tested; they range from trivial to a few hard ones that should be solvable with the given background. Readers must work through a significant number of exercises — the author insists on active problem-solving as the primary learning mechanism (tongue-in-cheek threat: 'If you attempt to read this without working through a significant number of exercises ... I will come to your house and pummel you with [Gr-EGA]').

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep geometric motivation / connect abstractions to examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be seduced by ... untethered abstraction. Hold tight to your geometric motivation as you learn the formal structures which have proved to be so effective in studying fundamental questions. When introduced to a new idea, always ask why you should care. Try at least to apply any new abstraction to some concrete example you can understand well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constantly seek concrete examples (affine complex varieties as central examples) and test abstractions against them; demand eventual motivation for abstractions even if not immediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite background
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader should be familiar with some basic notions in commutative ring theory, in particular the notion of ideals (including prime and maximal ideals) and localization. Tensor products and exact sequences of A-modules will be important. Some experience with field theory will be helpful from time to time. Some previous exposure to topology is certainly essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended companion references: Eisenbud [E], Atiyah–MacDonald [AtM], Matsumura [Mat2] for commutative algebra; Weibel [Wei] for homological algebra. The book aims to require as little background as possible but expects these basics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical sequencing: teach foundations (category theory, sheaves) early
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter 1. Category theory is only language, but it is language with an embedded logic. ... Chapter 2. The theory of sheaves again abstracts something you already understand well ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include Chapters 1–2 early in a course rather than relegating them to appendices; these foundations enable cleaner thinking and make later material accessible. Emphasize Yoneda’s Lemma and the idea of understanding objects via maps to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course adaptation and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: If you use this book for a course, you should of course adapt it to your own point of view and your own interests. In particular, you should think about an application or theorem you want to reach at the end of the course (which may well not be in this book), and then work toward it. You should feel no compulsion to sprint to the end; I advise instead taking more time, and ending at the right place for your students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors should choose endpoints (e.g., curves or the 27 lines on a cubic surface), use Figure 0.1 to plan dependencies, and be willing to omit or reorder material to suit students and semester length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of generality vs clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: For the most part, we will state results in the maximal generality that the proof justifies, but we will not give a much harder proof where the generality of the stronger result will not be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State theorems in the greatest generality justified by the proof, but avoid proving harder generalizations solely for generality's sake. When greater generality helps clarity or memory, include it, otherwise prefer simpler statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use minimal hypotheses; Noetherian only when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, I like having as few hypotheses as possible. Certainly a hypothesis that isn’t necessary to the proof is a red herring. ... Noetherian hypotheses are handy when necessary, but are otherwise misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce Noetherian conditions only when needed; introduce the notion 'quasiseparated' early since it clarifies where Noetherian hypotheses are actually used. Distinguish coherent vs finite-type quasicoherent sheaves explicitly so readers know which hypotheses are used in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology ordering: Čech before derived functors
rubrics_metrics.description: Cohomology is done first using the Čech approach (as Serre first did), and derived functor cohomology is introduced only later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present Čech cohomology as the first approach to give intuition and hands-on computations; later introduce derived functors once homological algebra is understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starred sections indicate optional material
rubrics_metrics.description: There are optional starred sections of topics worth knowing on a second or third (but not first) reading. They are marked with a star: ⋆. Starred sections are not necessarily harder, merely unimportant. You should not read double-starred sections (⋆⋆) unless you really really want to, but you should be aware of their existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ⋆ sections for later deepening; skip ⋆⋆ sections on first pass. The notation signals pedagogical priority, not difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include pathological examples and counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathological examples are useful to know. ... Pathologies and (counter)examples serve a similar goal. They also serve as a reality check, when confronting a new statement, theorem, or conjecture, whose veracity you may doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include counterexamples and pathologies as warning signs ('tall sticks on the sides of the road') to show limits of theorems and to illustrate subtlety in definitions; use them pedagogically to prevent overreliance on misleading special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple sources and comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: When working through a book in algebraic geometry, it is particularly helpful to have other algebraic geometry books at hand, to see different approaches and to have alternate expositions when things become difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this book as a core resource but consult complementary texts (Liu, GW, Stacks project) for alternative viewpoints and details omitted here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions and notational assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: All rings are assumed to be commutative unless explicitly stated otherwise. All rings are assumed to contain a unit, denoted 1. We accept the axiom of choice. We will use the notation (A, m) or (A, m, k) for local rings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the book's global conventions (e.g., about rings, 0-ring acceptance, axiom of choice). Nonmathematical conventions: 'Unimportant' is relative to the exposition. Be aware of where the author uses idiosyncratic wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended learning method: active/group learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Most mortals cannot learn algebraic geometry fully on their own; ideally you should read in a group, and even if not, you should have someone you can ask questions to (both stupid and smart questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer group study or seminars; seek mentors and peers to discuss exercises and conceptual difficulties rather than attempting solitary self-study only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize morphisms and categorical viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: One of Grothendieck’s fundamental lessons is that the morphisms are central. Important geometric properties should really be understood as properties of morphisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach and learn to view geometric notions (separatedness, properness, smoothness, etc.) primarily as properties of maps rather than as isolated properties of spaces; use categorical language to clarify concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a manageable canon and be explicit about goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Our intent is to cover a canon completely and rigorously, with enough examples and calculations to help develop intuition ... The core of the material should be digestible over a single year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set clear course goals (a canon to be mastered in a year), be explicit about which topics are essential vs optional, and plan course content accordingly; accept that the book is not encyclopedic and instructors will make compromises.
